'''Nashwa Abo Alhassan Eassa''' ({{Langx|ar|نشوى أبو الحسن عيسى}}) is a nano-[[Particle physics|particle physicist]] from [[Sudan]]. She is an assistant professor of physics ''and'' Dean of the Deanship of Scientific Research at [[Al-Neelain University]] in [[Khartoum]].<ref name="nashwa"/><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Sa’id |first1=Rabia Salihu |last2=Fuwape |first2=Ibiyinka |last3=Dikandé |first3=Alain Moise |last4=Mimouni |first4=Jamal |last5=Hasford |first5=Francis |last6=Haynes |first6=Delia |last7=Gledhill |first7=Igle |last8=Amolo |first8=George |last9=Akin-Ojo |first9=Omololu |last10=Eassa |first10=Nashwa |date=October 2020 |title=Physics in Africa |journal=Nature Reviews Physics |language=en |volume=2 |issue=10 |pages=520–523 |doi=10.1038/s42254-020-0239-8 |pmid=33728404 |pmc=7500249 |bibcode=2020NatRP...2..520S |issn=2522-5820}}</ref>

==Education==
Eassa received her BSc in physics from the [[University of Khartoum]] in 2004. In Sudan, those who wish to seek further education must study abroad, for women this is difficult for both financial reasons and cultural ones restricting women from traveling. Despite this she earned her [[Master of Science]] in [[nanotechnology]] and [[materials physics]] from Sweden's [[Linköping University]] in 2007. During her time at Linköping, tuition fees were not an issue for international students, however she still needed to manage her living expenses. To support her needs she worked at McDonald’s and distributed advertising to make a living for her work. <ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Bergstedt |first=Eva |title=Honorary doctor from Sudan fighting for women in academia |url=https://liu.se/en/news-item/hedersdoktor-fran-sudan-kampar-for-fler-kvinnor-inom-akademin |access-date=2024-11-18 |website=liu.se |language=en}}</ref>

Through a OWSD PhD Fellowship she was able to attend and graduate [[Nelson Mandela University|Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University]] from August 2008 to September 2012. During the first year of her stay she had given birth to her first child which made it difficult.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2015-07-01 |title=We need Women in Decision-Making Positions |url=https://owsd.net/about-owsd/impact/success-stories/we-need-women-decision-making-positions |access-date=2024-11-18 |website=OWSD |language=en}}</ref>

In August of 2008, the OSWD PhD fellowship motivated her to continue her studies in South Africa. She was able to balance the demands of her studies, motherhood, and marriage. Despite a demanding supervisor, she completed her PhD and gained valuable research experience which was unavailable in Sudan due to a lack of facilities.<ref name=":0" /> Her achievements at Linköping University earned her the honorary doctorate by the Faculty of Science and Engineering at Linköping, in recognition of her support to women who would want to further their education in research in Sudan. She emphasizes her want to help women in many places not only in Sudan, but also in Egypt, Yemen, Ghana, Benin, and Syria. Reflecting on her experience she states, “Support from other women in the academic world may be decisive to them continuing their career.”<ref name=":1" /> Nanosctructures: study the luminescence from InAs/GalnSb and InGaAs/InAsSb [[quantum well]] and also superlattice structures in order to investigate band alignments and interface quality.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-06-15 |title=Eassa Nashwa |url=https://owsd.net/member/eassa-nashwa-6 |access-date=2025-04-12 |website=OWSD |language=en}}</ref> 

==Career==
She has been a lecturer and assistant professor of physics at [[Neelain University|Al-Neelain University]] since 2007. She earned her PhD from [[Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University]] (NMMU) in 2012. Since 2013, Eassa is pursuing a post-doctoral fellowship in [[nanophotonics]] at NMMU. She founded the [[non-governmental organization]] Sudanese Women in Sciences in 2013 and is a member of Organization for Women in Science for the Developing World's South African Institute of Physics.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Mwaniki|first1=Joy|title=Five African Female Scientists You Should Definitely Know About|url=http://issues.ayibamagazine.com/five-african-female-scientists-you-should-definitely-know-about/|work=Ayiba Magazine|date=1 July 2015|access-date=8 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181018001128/http://issues.ayibamagazine.com/five-african-female-scientists-you-should-definitely-know-about|archive-date=18 October 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> From 2016 to 2020, Eassa also held the title of Vice President of the "Arab Region of Organization for Women Scientist in Developing World<ref>{{Cite book |date=December 2015 |title=2015 10th International Conference for Internet Technology and Secured Transactions (ICITST) |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/icitst.2015.7412040 |publisher=IEEE |pages=14 |doi=10.1109/icitst.2015.7412040 |chapter=Keynote speakers |isbn=978-1-9083-2052-0 }}</ref>

In 2015, Eassa won the [[Elsevier Foundation Award]] for Early Career Women Scientists in the Developing World. The award recognized her research on lessening film accumulation on the surface of high-speed semiconductors.<ref name="nashwa">{{cite web | url=http://www.aaas.org/news/early-career-women-scientists-developing-countries-honored-aaas-annual-meeting | title=Early-Career Women Scientists From Developing Countries Honored at AAAS Annual Meeting | publisher=Advance Science, Serving Society | date=14 February 2015 | accessdate=4 July 2015 | author= Wren, Kathy}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Venton|first1=Danielle|title=Tough As Nails: Female Scientists Rise Up In Nigeria|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2015/02/17/386549295/tough-as-nails-women-scientists-rise-up-in-nigeria|work=NPR|date=17 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.asianscientist.com/2015/02/topnews/vietnamese-mathematician-wins-elsevier-foundation-award/ | title=Vietnamese Mathematician Wins Elsevier Foundation Award |work=Asian Scientist Magazine | date=24 February 2015 | accessdate=4 July 2015}}</ref>

Eassa is involved in the development of [[nanotube]] structures and titanium oxide nanoparticles. She is also involved in projects to develop methods to split water molecules for hydrogen collection and to sanitize water with solar radiation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Women Scientists in Developing Countries Receive Elsevier Foundation Awards for Physics and Math|url=http://www.elsevier.com/about/press-releases/corporate-social-responsibility/women-scientists-in-developing-countries-receive-elsevier-foundation-awards-for-physics-and-math|publisher=Elsevier|date=10 February 2015}}</ref><ref name="nashwa"/>

She has been a candidate as Arab Countries Vice-President for Organization for Women in Science for the Developing World.<ref>{{cite web |title=Eassa Nashwa Elected Vice-President {{!}} OWSD |url=https://owsd.net/eassa-nashwa-elected-vice-president |website=owsd.net |accessdate=1 March 2019 |archive-date=2 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190302090554/https://owsd.net/eassa-nashwa-elected-vice-president |url-status=dead }}</ref>

As an Assistant Professor in Khartoum, her achievements include awards like the Elsevier Award and the Lindau Prize. These awards brought international visibility and opportunities. She improved training opportunities and fosters support through industries like an OWSD National Chapter for the next generation of women scientists in Sudan. <ref name=":0" />

Nashwa is a Sudanese woman physicist who overcame cultural and academic challenges to achieve international recognition. In Sudan, societal norms restrict women’s independence, but she pursued her passion for physics despite its limited resources and lack of stability.<ref name=":0" />

== Publications ==
Eassa's professional work appears in publications from journals like the African Journal of Engineering and the 2021 International Congress of Advanced Technology and Engineering.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Emam |first1=Reem |last2=Eassa |first2=Nashwa |date=2021-07-12 |title=Synthesis, Characterization and Size Evaluation of Biosynthesized Silver Nanoparticles by UV–Vis Spectroscopy |journal=African Journal of Engineering & Technology |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |doi=10.47959/AJET.2021.1.1.5 |doi-access=free |issn=2744-5151}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Adam |first1=Ali A. |last2=Elhag |first2=Nihad A. A. |last3=Saeed |first3=Fakhreldeen Abbas |last4=Yagob |first4=Mohamed |last5=Mohamed |first5=Fayha |last6=Eassa |first6=N. |last7=Abdalaziz |first7=Hanaa S. |last8=Ahmed |first8=M. A. |last9=Babiker |first9=Sharief F. |chapter=An Ensemble Machine Learning Model to Investigate the Screening System for Identification of Potential Patients with COVID-19 in Sudan |date=2021-07-04 |title=2021 International Congress of Advanced Technology and Engineering (ICOTEN) |publisher=IEEE |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1109/ICOTEN52080.2021.9493517 |isbn=978-1-6654-1224-7}}</ref> Aside from her publications on nanoparticles, she has also integrated her push for "gender equality" and the "gender gap in science and technology" in articles like her 2015 "Development of Sudanese Women in Physics".<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Eassa |first1=Nashwa |last2=Elmardi |first2=Maye |last3=Adam |first3=Buthaina |last4=Elgadi |first4=Mayada |last5=Abass |first5=Sara |date=2015 |title=Development of Sudanese women in physics |journal=Women in Physics: 5th Iupap International Conference on Women in Physics |series=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1702 |issue=1 |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/acp/article/824532 |pages=060040 |doi=10.1063/1.4937687|bibcode=2015AIPC.1697f0040E }}</ref> 

== Advocacy work ==
Eassa has contributed to multiple works detailing the roadblocks African scientists face. Eassa states that the African government's lack of attention to scientific research is the main cause of the low funding that researchers receive. <ref name=":2" />This trickles down to individual researchers not developing the skills they need and working in poor research environments.Eassa has also conducted research on the demographic of female physicists in Sudan. The research, conducted at Al Neelain University in Khartoum, highlights a university where the enrollment of female undergraduate physics students is double that of male students. Eassa collected data about the female students' interest in continuing their post-secondary education journeys and the effects of financial hardships on that decision. This research showed that an overwhelming number of female physicists at the university held lecturer positions due to the lack of female physicists attaining higher degrees.<ref name=":3" />
